students with comorblid mental health problems reported the most negative social contexts and were the most likely to receive special education services in comparison with students with other mental health problems.

youth with mental health needs have more difficulty in all three social contexts than youth who do not have mental health needs, and youth with internalizing problems have more difficulty with family and school context than youth with externalizing and no mental health needs.
youth with internalizing and externalizing problems reported more negative perceptions of their social contexts than did youth with no mental health problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
youth with mental health disorders experience a variety of negative social contexts that are not experienced by youth without mental health problems.
youth with comorbid mental health problems are at risk for negative outcomes in family and peer contexts, and for feeling anonymous and less well liked in the school context.
students with internalizing disorders, and especially those with comorbid disorders, were more likely than other students to have negative family, peer, and/or school experiences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
students with mental health problems have different perceptions of their social contexts and that these differences are related to their mental health profiles.
